c.tagline: Nigeria's purpose-built capital of green hills, monuments and unhurried calm.

taxi.fareNote: Meters are rarely used — agree the fare before setting off, or use ride-hailing apps (Uber, Bolt) for transparent, prepaid pricing.

emergency.note: 112 is Nigeria's toll-free unified emergency number for police, ambulance and fire; the FCT also runs a dedicated emergency line (112 or 767) that routes to Abuja responders.

english.label: Easy to get by in English

avoid.reason: Safer than Lagos but caution at night; kidnapping risk on some highways out of the city

hood_desc: Abuja's most prestigious district, home to embassies, senior officials and the city's top hotels, with upscale restaurants, food markets, malls and much of the nightlife; a secure, polished base for international visitors.

The commercial heartbeat of the city, packed with banks, corporate offices, restaurants, malls and a dense cluster of mid-range hotels; the most popular and convenient base for first-time visitors who want to be in the middle of everything.

An exclusive, heavily secured residential district east of the centre housing federal ministers and most of the diplomatic community; calm, leafy and low-key, best for travellers who value privacy and safety over nightlife.

The monumental core of the planned capital, laid out around the National Mosque, National Christian Centre, Millennium Park and the ministries, with government-grade hotels and business towers; walkable to Abuja's landmark sights.

One of Abuja's oldest and busiest districts just south of the centre, a dense mix of commercial and residential blocks with the sprawling Garki Market, ministries and reasonably priced hotels; a practical, well-connected base.

water.note: Drink bottled or filtered water only.

transit.hours: The Abuja Rail Mass Transit runs roughly 7:00 AM to 8:00 PM with trains every 30-45 minutes; AUMTCO buses and keke tricycles run from dawn until around 9-10 PM, with ride-hailing apps the safer option after dark.
transit.note: Abuja is a spread-out planned city; the light rail links the city centre, stadium and Nnamdi Azikiwe airport but coverage is limited, so most visitors rely on ride-hailing apps (Uber, Bolt), green city taxis and Keke NAPEP tricycles for short hops.
transit.pay: Rail tickets are bought at station counters (fares roughly ₦500-₦3,500 by distance and class); AUMTCO buses, keke tricycles and taxis are cash-only, paid to the driver in small naira notes, while ride-hailing rides are paid in-app or cash.

train: Abuja Rail Mass Transit (urban light rail)

Airport taxi to the city centre (45-60 min depending on traffic)

tip.r: Not traditionally expected but increasingly common in upscale hotels and restaurants (~10%); rounding up for taxi and ride-hailing drivers is standard.

food.name: Jollof Rice
food.desc: Long-grain rice simmered down in a smoky pepper, tomato and onion base, served with fried plantain and grilled chicken or beef.

places.name: Rodo
places.note: Abuja crowd favourite; the clay-pot smoky jollof with yaji chicken is its signature.

places.name: Nkoyo
places.note: Upmarket Nigerian dining by the water, strongly rated for jollof and grills.

places.name: Otega Restaurant
places.note: Open around the clock for jollof, stews and swallow at everyday prices.

food.name: Suya
food.desc: Thin beef or ram skewers coated in yaji, the groundnut-and-chilli spice rub, grilled over charcoal and served with raw onion and tomato.

places.name: Yahuza Suya Spot
places.note: One of Abuja's longest-standing suya names, busy from nightfall.

places.name: Suya on the Spot
places.note: Sit-down suya house also doing masa, miyan taushe and pepper soup.

places.name: Aminu Kano Crescent suya stalls
places.note: Street grills that fill from about 8pm and sell out; the classic Abuja suya run.

food.name: Pounded Yam with Egusi
food.desc: Smooth pounded yam swallow eaten by hand with egusi, a thick melon-seed soup cooked with bitterleaf, palm oil, goat meat and stockfish.

places.name: Jevinik Restaurant
places.note: Well-known native-soup house serving egusi, ogbono and bitterleaf with swallow.

places.name: Otega Restaurant
places.note: Round-the-clock kitchen with the full range of swallows and traditional soups.

places.name: Nkoyo
places.note: Polished versions of the Nigerian soup classics in a lakeside setting.

food.name: Pepper Soup
food.desc: Fiery clear broth of catfish, goat or assorted meat spiced with uziza, ehuru and scotch bonnet; a restorative eaten hot in a bowl.

places.name: Nkoyo
places.note: Catfish pepper soup and grilled fish are among its most ordered plates.

places.name: Otega Restaurant
places.note: Goat and fish pepper soups on the menu at any hour of the night.

places.name: Jevinik Restaurant
places.note: Traditional Nigerian kitchen known for deeply spiced pepper soups.

food.name: Moin Moin and Akara
food.desc: Peeled black-eyed beans blended with pepper and onion, then steamed into savoury moin moin pudding or deep-fried into akara balls.

places.name: Wuse Market food stalls
places.note: Market cooks sell moin moin, akara and pap from early morning at low prices.

places.name: Otega Restaurant
places.note: Bean dishes served alongside the rice and swallow plates all day.

places.name: Jevinik Restaurant
places.note: Traditional sides including moin moin accompany its soup and swallow menu.

food.name: Masa and Miyan Taushe
food.desc: Northern Nigerian staples: puffy fermented rice cakes fried in a dimpled pan, eaten with a pumpkin and groundnut stew.

places.name: Suya on the Spot
places.note: One of the easiest places in Abuja to try masa and miyan taushe sit-down.

places.name: The Charcoal Grill
places.note: Focused on straightforward northern Nigerian grills and traditional plates.

places.name: Wuse Market food stalls
places.note: Hausa vendors fry masa to order beside the market's spice and grain sellers.

food.name: Zobo and Kunu
food.desc: Zobo, a tart hibiscus infusion with ginger and pineapple, and kunu, a lightly spiced millet or sorghum drink; both non-alcoholic staples.

places.name: Rodo
places.note: House zobo and other Nigerian coolers served with the clay-pot mains.

places.name: Suya on the Spot
places.note: Kunu and zobo are the traditional chasers to a plate of yaji-spiced suya.

places.name: Wuse Market food stalls
places.note: Bottles of home-brewed zobo and kunu sold cheaply throughout the market.

food.name: Palm Wine and Nigerian Lager
food.desc: Fresh-tapped palm wine, cloudy and lightly fizzy, plus cold Star or Gulder lager; note much of northern Nigeria beyond Abuja is dry.

places.name: Nkoyo
places.note: Lakeside restaurant and bar pouring palm wine alongside Nigerian beers.

places.name: Otega Restaurant
places.note: 24-hour spot where palm wine and lager accompany the pepper soup crowd.

places.name: The Charcoal Grill
places.note: Open-air grill house, a standard stop for cold beer with suya and asun.

landmarks: Aso Rock
This massive dome-shaped monolith looms over the city and gives Abuja its nickname, offering dramatic views and a hiking route to its summit.
Zuma Rock
A colossal 725-meter monolith just outside the city that has become the unofficial gateway symbol to Abuja, famous for the natural face-like formation on its surface.
Abuja National Mosque
With its golden dome and four slender minarets, this is one of the largest mosques in West Africa and a striking symbol of the capital's skyline.
National Christian Centre
This soaring cathedral with a distinctive spire complements the National Mosque as a symbol of Nigeria's religious diversity and is a favorite photo subject.
Millennium Park
Designed by renowned architect Manfredi Nicoletti, this is Abuja's largest public park, known for its ornamental gates, waterways, and green open spaces.
Nigerian National Assembly Complex
The seat of Nigeria's federal legislature, instantly recognizable by its green dome and a must-see stop for anyone interested in the nation's governance.
Jabi Lake
A scenic man-made lake ringed by a boardwalk, restaurants, and boating facilities, offering some of Abuja's best sunset photography.
Transcorp Hilton Abuja
An iconic five-star hotel and city landmark near the presidential villa, long a gathering point for dignitaries and a recognizable feature of the skyline.
Abuja City Gate
A monumental arch structure that has become a symbolic entrance marker to the city, popular for photos especially when lit up at night.
Gurara Falls
A powerful, wide waterfall just outside Abuja that makes for a spectacular natural day trip and one of the region's most photographed sights.

dom.op: Nigerian Railway Corporation - Abuja-Kaduna Train Service

train.note: Abuja's long-distance trains use Idu station on the northern edge of the city rather than anywhere central, and the standard-gauge Abuja-Kaduna service covers the 186 km in about two hours - the usual way to reach Kaduna without driving a highway with a bad security record. Seats sell out quickly and are booked through the NRC's dedicated AKTS e-ticketing portal rather than at the window. The Abuja light rail connects Idu with the city centre and Nnamdi Azikiwe airport; it was suspended for years and only resumed running in May 2024. There are no international passenger trains anywhere in Nigeria.

bus.note: Intercity coaches leave from motor parks such as Jabi, Utako and Kugbo rather than a single central station, with ABC Transport (https://www.abctransport.com/) and GIGM (https://gigm.com/) the most reliable operators and both bookable online. Lagos is roughly 9-11 hours away, Kaduna 2-3 hours and Enugu about 7 hours, and night departures are best avoided. No coach runs directly abroad from Abuja - ABC Transport's cross-border services to Accra, Cotonou and Lome all start from its Jibowu terminal in Lagos, so you connect there.

ferry.note: Abuja sits on the inland plateau of central Nigeria with no navigable waterway serving the city, so there are no passenger boat or ferry services of any kind.

half.name: Usuma Dam
half.blurb: Reservoir and hiking area outside the capital offering trails, picnic spots, and canoe rides across calm water.

full.name: Kajuru Castle
full.blurb: Turreted medieval-style castle on a mountaintop near Kaduna, built by a Nigerian chief and open for tours and swimming.
